success_patterns: The winning option was the plain, natural theorem statement in the stem's own vocabulary. Every distractor was a single edit of it: an added hypothesis or proviso, a dropped hypothesis, a shifted constant, an inflated uniformity or dependence clause, or a downgrade to a weaker conclusion.

The agent stopped at the pivot between 'true but weaker' and 'sharper but unjustified'. It rejected a bare 'finitely many' or 'merely metrizable' when the exact bound or explicit construction was the natural result. It also rejected a sharpened constant (6g-6 for 6g), a two-sided estimate, 'every weak solution', and uniform-in-T constants.

Riders were killed by conflict with a standard structural fact, not by taste. Fixed ellipticity forces a Hölder exponent bounded below, so an exponentially small exponent needs ellipticity that grows with γ. Boundary solutions behave like dist^s, so regularity beyond C^s is impossible. A totally geodesic surface lies in a smaller subgroup, so it is not Zariski dense. A single universal object cannot depend on the order A.

Construction-recipe riders were rejected ('only a metric on E(S)', 'only finitely many weighted terms', 'without auxiliary metrics'). The faithful claim was the bare 'an explicit compatible metric exists', which beats the bare 'is metrizable'.

In near-duplicate formula options, the correct one was the hub. The others differed from it by one edit: halving a different term, widening a sum from odd l to all l, or changing 'only one' to 'at most one'. Tidy symmetric variants (both terms halved, both terms full) were the corruptions, since the stem treats the two types differently.

patch.reasoning: The skill already covers the hub test, rider falsification and the strength ladder. These trajectories add three habits worth making explicit. First, falsify riders by conflict with a standard structural theorem or model example, rather than by plausibility. Second, treat 'how it is built' clauses as corruptions, while still preferring explicit-construction over bare existence when the construction is standard. Third, in formula-variant options, do not symmetrize or tidy the coefficients, and do not use 'at most one' as a hedge when existence is guaranteed.

edits.content: - Structural-conflict test for riders: ask whether a rider contradicts a standard theorem or a model example in the stem's own setting. (a) A claim of a fixed or bounded ellipticity/constant together with a degenerate conclusion (exponent -> 0 exponentially, constants blowing up) contradicts compactness or De Giorgi-Nash-Moser type lower bounds; the valid version lets the ellipticity grow with the degeneracy parameter. (b) Regularity better than the optimal model behaviour (e.g. beyond C^s at a boundary where solutions behave like dist^s) is false. (c) 'Comes from a totally geodesic / subgroup-contained object' contradicts Zariski density or thinness. (d) A single object 'independent of the choice' contradicts the stem when the data varies. Reject the option the moment one such conflict is found, even if it looks sharper.

edits.target: ## Near-duplicate options: constants, quantifiers, ranges, exact details
edits.content: - Recipe riders: clauses saying HOW the object is built or WHAT it uses ('only from a metric on the base', 'with only finitely many correction terms', 'without any auxiliary data', 'can always be obtained from ...') are inflated or altered corruptions unless derivable. The faithful claim states the object and its defining property ('an explicit metric inducing exactly the stated topology'). That claim still beats a bare 'is metrizable / exists' when the construction is standard from the stem's data, since the stronger clause is derivable. Likewise, do not add a regime or class restriction ('provided the parameters are distinct') that the stem's hypotheses do not need.

edits.target: ## Near-duplicate options: constants, quantifiers, ranges, exact details
edits.content: - Formula-variant options (same equation, different coefficients, sum ranges or solution-count wording): list the options as single edits of one hub. Typical edits are a halved vs full term, odd l vs all l, 'only one' vs 'at most one', and the same weight on two types. Do not prefer the more symmetric or tidier formula. If the stem treats two types differently (e.g. Type O vs Type I), expect different coefficients. 'Has only one solution' is the natural uniqueness phrasing when existence is built into the data, so 'at most one' is a hedge, not the safer answer. Confirm the coefficient with a one-block or one-dimensional sanity case.
